newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Ethiopia seeks to renegotiate Russian loans.
newsitem.headline: Ethiopia seeks to renegotiate Russian loans.

text.p: Impoverished Ethiopia said on Friday it was negotiating the repayment of three billion Russian roubles lent to the Soviet-backed government of ousted dictator Mengistu Haile Mariam.

But Finance Minister Sufian Ahmed told reporters the debt posed a "moral dilemma" for the government of Prime Minister Meles Zenawi because the money was used to acquire arms to devastate the Horn of Africa nation.
"Ethiopia is still negotiating and will make every effort to convince Russia that the military debt should be cancelled," the minister said.

He added: "Payment of the former Soviet loan taken by the previous government for arms purchases, which is contrary to the peaceful policy of the Federal Government of Ethiopia, raises serious moral issues.
"One must understand that the military debt was not used for development but rather to devastate the nation," he said.
Mengistu spent untold billions trying to suppress rebellions in northern Ethiopia and was one of Moscow's staunchest supporters against Western influence in Africa.
Mengistu, who now lives in exile in Zimbabwe, was widely known as the Black Stalin to his people.
The present rulers drove Mengistu from the capital in 1991 in an uprising that ushered in free market reforms, Western aid and independence for Eritrea.
Ethiopia also owes Moscow separate monies in development and economic aid.
Sufian hailed the country's free market reforms, saying they had attracted growth and reversed decline under Mengistu.

The minister also praised a recent 67 percent debt reduction granted by the Paris Club group of donors saying it was a result of "success in Ethiopia's economic reform measures and subsequent signs of macro-economic stability."
Ethiopia's external debt stands at $4.4 billion.
He said Ethiopia, for years a food-deficit nation, achieved self-sufficiency in food production for the first time this year.
The country produced a bumper harvest of 11.7 million tonnes in the 1996/97 crop year, far exceeding an estimated 8.7 million tonnes required to feed the country's 55 million.
